5 questions — Recommend and prioritize physical and managerial controls (CED 2.3.A–2.3.B)

column4: >Answer each question, then check your score below

column1: Xtensr Research Labs · Delmar Applied Optics

Xtensr Research Labs is acquiring Delmar Applied Optics, and you are on the physical security team writing the control recommendations for the new site. The walkthrough already recorded the findings: a finished-lens vault, an engineering file server in a utility closet, a reception PC on the internal wireless network, a badge controller cabinet in the open lobby, a testing bay on one power panel, and an optics bay below street grade on a floodplain. Five recommendations now need your judgment.

During the Delmar walkthrough, a technician badged into the engineering wing and a stranger followed through the door behind him. The technician never saw the door close. Xtensr must recommend one control that would have stopped this entry even if the technician stayed unaware. Which recommendation does the control’s own function support?

EK 2.3.B.5 — access control vestibules and turnstiles prevent an authorized person from intentionally or accidentally admitting an unauthorized person. That is the only one of the four that works when the authorized employee does not know anyone is behind him: the vestibule physically admits one authenticated person per cycle.

(A) Incorrect — EK 2.3.A.1 training tells employees not to badge others in, which addresses piggybacking, where the employee knowingly grants access. This entry was tailgating: no awareness, so there was no decision for training to change.

(B) Incorrect — EK 2.3.B.4 card readers deny unlisted badges and record use, but the door was already open on a valid badge. This control would document the technician’s entry and detect nothing about the second person.
(D) Incorrect — EK 2.3.B.3 a cabinet lock protects the server if someone reaches it, but it does nothing about who gets into the wing.
Exam Tip: When a stem tells you what the employee did or did not notice, it is testing consent. Training and policy reach decisions employees make
column2: vestibules and turnstiles reach entries they never see.

Delmar’s reception PC sits in an area anyone may walk into, connects to the internal wireless network, and has exposed USB ports. Xtensr considers three recommendations:

  I. Disable the USB ports on the reception PC.
  II. Require the receptionist to lock the workstation before leaving it unattended and to clear sensitive documents from the desk.
  III. Install bollards along the parking-lot edge of the reception entrance.

Which recommendations reduce the risk that this PC becomes a foothold into other Delmar resources?

I is EK 2.3.B.6 — disabling USB ports stops an external drive from loading malware onto the machine. II is EK 2.3.A.2 — a workstation security policy requires locking the device before leaving it unattended and clearing sensitive documents, which closes the unattended logged-in session. Both attack the foothold directly. III does not: bollards are a perimeter deterrent.
(A) Incorrect — I is correct but incomplete. An adversary who never touches a USB port can still sit down at an unlocked, logged-in session, which is what II prevents.
(C) Incorrect — II is correct but III is not. Under EK 2.3.B.2, bollards deter a vehicle or a person from approaching the building
column2: the reception area is already open to visitors by design.

column1: (D) Incorrect — including III treats every physical control as relevant to every risk. Bollards would not change anything about a networked PC with open ports inside the lobby.
Exam Tip: On a roman-numeral item, test each statement against the exact risk named in the stem — here, a foothold on one machine. A control can be a real control and still be the wrong control.

Delmar’s optics bay sits below street grade on a floodplain, and the testing bay next to it draws power from a single panel that has tripped twice this year. Which recommendation would do the LEAST to protect the availability of the testing bay’s equipment?

A turnstile is a real control — EK 2.3.B.5 — but it addresses unauthorized entry into a restricted space, not availability. The other three all keep the equipment running or intact: a UPS and a generator answer the power threat (EK 2.3.B.7) and relocating the racks answers the flood, which EK 2.2.B.1 counts as a threat because natural disasters damage devices and disrupt services.
(A) Incorrect — EK 2.3.B.7 a UPS provides backup power for a device during an outage, which is exactly the panel-trip problem in the stem.
(B) Incorrect — EK 2.3.B.7 generators supply power at building scale to a set of critical devices, covering an outage longer than a UPS can bridge.
(D) Incorrect — moving the racks above the flood line removes the equipment from the hazard, which protects availability even though no power control is involved.

Exam Tip: Match the control to the principle the stem names. LEAST questions are usually won by noticing that three options serve the named principle and one serves a different one — here, confidentiality of a restricted space instead of availability.

Xtensr’s draft mitigation plan for Delmar ranks four recommendations. Exactly one row is ranked wrongly. Mitigations are prioritized by the severity of the risk and the cost of the mitigation.

  1. Lock on the utility closet holding the engineering file server — high severity, low cost
  2. Move the badge controller cabinet out of the open lobby into a locked enclosure — high severity, moderate cost
  3. Bollards around the full building perimeter — low severity, high cost
  4. Disable the USB ports on the reception PC — moderate severity, negligible cost

Which correction is BEST?

Rows 1, 2 and 3 are already ordered correctly: two high-severity risks first, cheapest of the two leading, and the low-severity high-cost item last among them. Row 4 is the error — a moderate-severity risk closed at negligible cost should come before a low-severity risk that costs the most of any row. EK 2.3.B.8 weighs severity and cost together, not severity alone.
(B) Incorrect — nothing in EK 2.3 makes perimeter controls a prerequisite for interior controls. A defense-in-depth strategy layers controls
column2: it does not require them in an outside-in order.

column1: (C) Incorrect — row 1 is the strongest row in the plan. EK 2.3.B.3 locks on server cabinets prevent devices from being accessed or stolen, and a high-severity risk closed at low cost is exactly what EK 2.3.B.8 puts first.
(D) Incorrect — the plan lists row 2 at moderate cost, not the highest cost, so the reason given is false. Cost alone would not settle the ranking anyway.
Exam Tip: On a spot-the-error item, find the error before you read the fixes. Three of these options repair a row that was already right, and each one sounds reasonable on its own.

A card reader on the finished-lens vault door denies any badge that is not on the vault access list and records which badge opened the door and when. Which statement BEST justifies this single control in the Delmar report?

EK 2.3.B.1 asks how a control prevents, detects, or corrects an attack, and EK 2.3.B.4 says card readers do two of those: they deny unauthorized badges and they record which badge was used at which entry at what time. Naming both functions is what justifies the control, and the recorded use is what makes a cloned or shared badge investigable afterward.
(A) Incorrect — a corrective control restores a system to an operational state. A log tells you a lens left the vault
column2: it does not bring the lens back.

column1: (B) Incorrect — no single control removes the need for the others. Under EK 2.1.G a layered defense uses several control types precisely so one failure does not open the asset.
(C) Incorrect — the reason is false for this room. Finished lenses are the site’s highest-value inventory, so EK 2.2.C.4 low-risk reasoning does not apply, and detection alone leaves the entry open.

Exam Tip: Card readers are the CED’s clearest example of a control with two functions. If an option credits a control with only one of its functions, or with a function it does not have, that is the flaw to find.
